section: 1. Your name is already written down
text: Place yourself in Jinju, in southeastern Korea, during the 1860s. You are an adult woman in an institution that trains and manages female performers. We are reconstructing that role from historical scholarship, rather than following the diary of one named woman. The ceremonies we reach are documented; the private thoughts of the woman standing inside them are not ours to invent.

section: 2. The register behind the performance
text: The word gisaeng can cover different experiences across different periods. For this story, keep one particular position in view: a government-affiliated performer in late Joseon.

section: 2. The register behind the performance
text: The Academy of Korean Studies' account explains that Joseon gisaeng were commonly of government nobi status. Nobi describes a historically specific form of unfree status. Here, the government connection is essential: these women belonged within a system of service and official supervision.

section: 2. The register behind the performance

section: 3. The work the audience does not see
text: The history is much older than your nineteenth-century setting. Female musical institutions are documented in Goryeo, and the scholarly accounts discuss earlier performance traditions as well. There is no need to invent a single founding day for all gisaeng history. By the time of our Jinju story, these institutions have already undergone substantial change.

section: 5. When the request comes from the capital
text: As a provincial performer, your institution belongs within a wider network. Local service and court service are connected, but they are not the same assignment.

section: 5. When the request comes from the capital
text: The scholarly account of female musical performance describes a major change after 1623. The court no longer maintained the earlier arrangement of resident professional female performers attached to its music office in the capital. For relevant court occasions, women could instead be selected from the provinces and returned afterwards.

text: The Academy's account of Uiam Byeolje describes a ceremony established in Jinju under the magistrate Jeong Hyeon-seok. It associates the occasion with Chokseokru, the pavilion at Jinju's fortress, and with the commemoration of Nongae.

section: 7. The woman at the centre of the ceremony
text: For the women participating, the occasion involved more than supplying entertainment alongside a ceremony. According to that account, local government-affiliated gisaeng filled the roles required to carry it out, including ritual, singing, dancing and musical roles.
